newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW - Intel Ireland paints rosy future.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Intel Ireland paints rosy future.

text.p: The head of Intel Ireland Ltd, the biggest supplier of semi-conductors to Europe, says locating in Ireland has proved very positive for the international high-technology conglomerate.

Intel Ireland's General Manager Frank McCabe, an Irishman born in the northern county of Monaghan, said the success of the Irish plant, which employs 4,000 people, was key to Intel's decision to build a new $1.5 billion state-of-the-art factory at its Leixlip site, close to Dublin.
Intel Ireland, the group's sole manufacturing centre for Europe, produced the world's first eight-inch wafers of pure silicon and is the biggest supplier of Pentium chips in the world.
Parent company Intel Corp, based in California's silicon valley, has committed a total of $2.5 billion to its Irish division's development.
"We choose Ireland because of its close proximity to Europe which is a very big market," McCabe told Reuters in a interview.
Its investment in Ireland is the biggest by any multinational and is trumpeted by the government as proof that Ireland is fast becoming the hi-tech centre of Europe.
He said other key factors were being able to hire the "best and the brightest" of Ireland's highly educated graduates in an environment conducive to agility, speed and flexibilty.

"If you think of many places in continental Europe they have a very bureaucratic system, imposed perhaps by the government, on how things should operate which often results in companies not being able to move at the speed needed," McCabe said.
Ireland also offers a special 10 percent corporation tax incentive which McCabe said was also a very important factor.
Europe accounts for more than a quarter of Intel's worldwide revenue "... so it is a very important part of the business".

McCabe would not be drawn on what the company would do if Ireland's low tax incentive, which is due to be reviewed in 2010, ceased. He merely pointed out that the Irish exchequer received large sums in tax revenue from multi-nationals like Intel Ireland despite the low tax rate.
Looking to the future McCabe said Europe should be concerned by rapid growth in high-tech assimilation going on in Asia.
Asia, he said, was the fastest growing part of the company, currently accounting for 30 percent of the group's $20.8 billion revenue.
"As a European, not in terms of Intel, that would be one of the things to be concerned about as Asia is adopting technology at a faster rate than Europe," McCabe said.
He said that the application of information technology would be one of the most important factors, from a competitive point of view, as the world nears the next century.
